newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia, Singapore war of words seen sputtering on.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia, Singapore war of words seen sputtering on.

text.p: Malaysia's war of words with Singapore may sputter on but Kuala Lumpur was not expected to take further action against a neighbour with whom it has intimate economic and cultural ties, analysts said.
But as the governments step back, the media of both countries had picked up the banner in this steam-venting exercise, they said.
Remarks by Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad last week indicated Malaysia wants to put the bitter row behind it.
"I don't want to prolong the matter," Mahathir told reporters. "It takes time to get over our feelings of hurt. I'll only go so far."
And Singaporean leaders, including Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, have said they will let Malaysia set the pace in repairing the worst diplomatic tiff in years between the neighbours.
Goh last month quoted an old Malay saying that even a sharp knife cannot cut water in two to explain how close the ties were between tow countries who share the same Imperial legacy.
Singapore is one of the largest investors in Malaysia, ploughing in $1.3 billion last year, and is its biggest trading partner, with two-way trade worth $34 billion last year.
Malaysia provides Singapore with most of its water and ships up to half of its exports through Singapore's port.
"It is better that the two countries move on," said an analyst at a Malaysian think-tank. "There is so much at stake here... the destinies of the two are entwined," he said.

Singapore's founding father and former prime minister Lee Kuan Yew unleashed a torrent of anger in Malaysia when he said the southern state of Johor was "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".
The remarks were contained in a court affidavit in his libel suit against an opposition leader and Lee said they were never meant to be public.

To soothe Malaysian anger, Lee in a rare move, offered an unreserved apology to Malaysians over the remarks. The Singapore High Court last week allowed him to delete the offending words from the affidavit.
Last Tuesday, The Straits Times fanned the fury when it published stories which said Lee was probably justified in his criticism of Johor as an unsafe place.
Malaysians reacted angrily, with trade minister Rafidah Aziz last week calling for a "media war" against Singapore.

Last Thursday, leading Malay daily Utusan Malaysia was sharply critical in a front page editorial, while Malaysia's New Straits Times daily carried an item about a United Nations report showing crime in Singapore to be higher than in Malaysia.

"I was a little bit surprised the Straits Times wanted to keep at it," said analyst Bruce Gale of the Political & Economic Risk Consultancy in Singapore. "What we see in the New Straits Times is a bit tit for tat," he said.
But on Sunday Singapore's pro-government Sunday Times said Singaporeans had no wish to antagonise Malaysians needlessly and wanted constructive talks on serious issues, not a pointless media war.
"Being pragmatic they (Singaporeans) would rather focus on more pressing concerns than engage in a pointless spat with their neighbours," the paper said in a commentary.
